From left: Utharaa Zacharias and Palaash Chaudhary of Soft-Geometry, Steffany Tran of Vy Voi, Minjae Kim, Aaron and Irisa Chan-Kawabi of Kawabi, and Dominik Tarabański (Image credit: Tracy Nguyen, Jingyu Lin) Jump to category: Soft Geometry Dominik Tarabański Vy Voi Minjae Kim Kawabi Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Artists and designers the world over continue to choose to make the US their home. As the latest newcomers in this ‘ nation of immigrants ' join a crowd of inspiring locals with dual heritage, their varied experiences help shape creative America. To celebrate the country's role as a meeting point of creative minds, we look at the plurality of voices contributing to its enduring crucible of culture and dynamism. We speak to five studios – whose founders (all Wallpaper* US400 honorees) have roots in Poland , Vietnam, India , South Korea and China , but who have made the US their creative base – about how their heritage influences their output. Meet a new generation of American designers Soft Geometry (Image credit: Tracy Nguyen) For many creatives, geography is less a fixed point than an inheritance, carried across borders and reimagined in new contexts. This is true for Utharaa Zacharias and Palaash Chaudhary, founders of Soft-Geometry, a practice that took root in India and found a fuller expression in the US, as the two became partners in work and life. (Image credit: Tracy Nguyen) A rich cultural potpourri is the core of their practice. ‘Palaash is from Ghaziabad, near Delhi, and I am from Kochi, Kerala; it would be hard to pick two places more diametrically opposite,' says Zacharias. Growing up, they spoke different languages, ate different food and were raised in different religions, but their friendship found common ground in design. It began in college in Delhi and continued at the Savannah College of Art and Design in Georgia, where working on projects revealed a shared aesthetic. One afternoon, they scribbled in a notebook that together they made ‘soft geometries'. Text by Aditi Sharma Read more Dominik Tarabański (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Dominik Tarabański was born in 1982 in Radymno, Poland, a small town near the Ukrainian border, and studied photography in Łódź and Warsaw. After four years moving between Polish cities, he left for New York in 2012. Heading to New York, he says, was like going to the moon; a single three-week visit decided it for him. Fashion photography paid the bills and took him between New York, Paris and London . The still lifes he made by hand, away from the crowded sets. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Tarabański says he is pursuing ‘this intersection of synthetic and organic', which sits ‘at the foundation of everything I do'. He contorts living matter into arrangements as deliberately impossible as a Dutch flower painting , then photographs them at the fleeting point of giving way. The finished prints are large, over 2m tall, and hold the wall like sculpture. From a rubber band and a dried stem, he makes what he calls a kind of magic: ‘Nothing becomes something.' Text by Reeme Idris Read more Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Vy Voi (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) For Steffany Tran, the Vietnamese-American founder of New York -based studio Vy Voi , objects become storytellers. Their materials, form and construction reflect longstanding cultural traditions, which she interprets through her own voice. ‘I describe my practice as almost like using a metal detector and finding nuggets in history,' she says. Tran, whose parents are both refugees, grew up between San José, California , and Saigon, where she spent summers visiting her family. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) After studying industrial design in the San Francisco Bay Area, Tran moved to New York, where she worked in traditional firms, where the fast pace and problem-solving briefs were not exactly aligned with her personal interest in the art of making. She then took up ceramics at a local community centre as a creative outlet and eventually, she decided to dedicate all her time to creating handmade objects inspired by Vietnamese craft, which she felt were missing from the contemporary design world. ‘It was almost an exercise in this idea of if you can't find it, build it yourself,' Tran says. Text by Diana Budds Read more Minjae Kim (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Seoul -born, New York-based designer Minjae Kim discovered the US on an exchange in high school. After studying painting and architecture, and a stint of military service back home, in 2008 he travelled to Seattle to continue his studies, later moving to New York for a Master of Architecture at Columbia University. He spent three years at Studio Giancarlo Valle, then started his own practice from the basement of his old apartment during the pandemic. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) His debut in 2021 at LA design gallery Marta catalogued Western typologies, such as a chair adapted from Freud's personal study. These were objects that differed from his understanding of the world, and he made them his by remaking them – for example, by treating fibreglass like cloth, quilting it before coating it with resin. Text by Reeme Idris Read more Kawabi (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Lanterns are talismanic in Chinese folklore. They are beacons that guide ancestral spirits, invite prosperity, and protect against malevolent forces. For Aaron and Irisa Chan-Kawabi, founders of New York studio Kawabi, they are also symbols of belonging. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Whenever the designers encountered these objects in the US, typically at Chinese restaurants or souvenir shops, they were the same symmetrical red or white design. ‘How does a typology move from one culture to another?' Aaron wondered. He and Irisa saw parallels to their own experience as part of the diaspora (Irisa was born in China and grew up in Massachusetts; Aaron was born in Brooklyn to parents who emigrated from Hong Kong ) and began to contemplate what a lantern that represented their own experience might look like. Photograph: Lorena Sopena Lopez/Anadolu/Getty Images Opinion Europe The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same Gordon Brown As Spain heads into a critical election, polling shows that many voters attracted by rightwing parties don’t really agree with their ideas Sat 21 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Last modified on Sat 21 Nov 2026 03.30 EST Share W hen Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France , Poland , Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism. Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states . Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east , Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south. Of the EU’s 27 countries, 21 are run from the centre or right. But there is a new danger, and it is not just that another extreme rightwing populist party, Spain’s Vox , may be on the point of entering government. It is also the capitulation of the centre-right parties to far-right policies, as the firewall separating the right from the extreme right starts to fall across the continent. Vox has proposed mass deportations of migrants under the banner of “remigration” . Spain’s Popular party (PP) has – as documented by an investigation published by LaSexta – been prepared to join with Vox in regional coalitions to remove gender-equality initiatives and minority-language protections, and to challenge abortion and LGBTQ+ protections . And although they disagree about its definition, the PP and Vox have both explicitly endorsed the principle of prioridad nacional – national preference in social security and health benefits. Just as worrying is the rise of a global coalition of anti-internationalists. Reports of an early, unpublished version of Donald Trump’s national security strategy last year envisaged direct support being offered from the US to Europe’s extreme populist nationalist parties. The White House denied those reports, but in August, Reuters also claimed the Trump administration planned to provide at least $25m (£19m) in funding for conservative civil-society initiatives in Europe, including $4m for rightwing media. Not content with stating via the national strategy document that Europe was threatened with “civilisational erasure”, Trump dispatched his vice-president, JD Vance, to consort with the extreme-right AfD party in Germany in preference to meeting the chancellor . Meanwhile, having convened in Hungary and the UK this year, the US-led Conservative Political Action Conference – which brings together conservative activists, commentators and officials – plans an even bigger “expansion into western Europe” with an Italian summit in 2027 . How to push back? One way is to exploit the truth: that what the far right offers isn’t necessarily in sync with what ordinary people want. Polling for the Rockefeller Foundation , of which I am a trustee, reveals the picture is much more nuanced if we ask Europeans what they are really feeling. Spain’s statutory minimum wage has increased by two-thirds and the proportion of workers on fixed-term contracts has fallen by more than 40% under the government of Pedro Sánchez. With more than half of Spain’s electricity now coming from renewables, energy price rises have hit less hard than elsewhere in Europe, and consumer confidence has been much higher. But Spain’s official polling agency, the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), found that only a third give a positive assessment of the economy, while earlier this month, concerns over housing and rents led to the country’s first general strike in 14 years along with mass demonstrations on the streets of its major cities. Indeed, across Europe, half of those polled say they don’t trust their government, while two-thirds say they are nostalgic for the past, believing their countries have lost touch with the values that built them. But these are surface manifestations of dissatisfaction. What really worries people in their daily lives? People fear economic decline – which can mean the sense that their country is doing badly ( 65% say theirs has got worse in the past year), as well as personal financial disappointment over the gap between their expectations and their current experience. Nearly 50% say they are worse off than they expected to be five years ago, with 59% worrying more about money every year. They also worry that nobody is there to stand up for them or speak up on their behalf. Half of respondents say that, in a crisis, people in their community would look out only for themselves. More telling, perhaps, is that half feel the government helps other groups more than theirs. What is striking is that, for many, this sense of civic decline, which is a more cultural phenomenon, matters as much as economic decline. But while it may mean they lend their votes to populist nationalist parties that claim to speak for their concerns, most are not populist nationalists at heart. Only 15% of those voting for the radical right take a consistently zero-sum view of the world – seeing the gains of one social group as necessarily coming at the expense of another. In Spain, only 12% of Vox voters are consistently zero-sum. And a total of 61% of respondents across the European countries polled are prepared to say they want their country to cooperate internationally, even when it means compromising on national interests. Even more, 80% , reject intolerant attitudes, believing that good solutions come from hearing many different viewpoints. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion What does this mean when it comes to actual votes? Across Europe, no more than 25% anywhere say they would vote for the radical right, and fewer – about 20% – see another ethnic group’s gain as their own loss. As few as 10% hold to the us-v-them mindset on trade, migration and technology that characterises the rhetoric and ideology of the populist movements. And despite the enormous publicity the issue receives, and legitimate concerns about illegal migration, fewer than 25% put managing migration among the top issues for countries to work on together. Anti-incumbent voting is now commonplace. Millions are open to voting for change when they are dissatisfied, and may choose to protest with a vote for the extreme right. Sánchez is defending a strong record at home and abroad . Despite the day-to-day polls, Spain has one of the smallest us-v-them blocs and the lowest radical-right vote of the countries we polled, with votes destined for the extreme right standing at 14%, well short of the PP and Sánchez’s Socialists. The general public in Spain and in Europe are unhappy with their economic plight and fear the loss of civic cohesion, but they have not, in the main, become converts to far-right ideology. The drift is not inevitable. By knowing how people really feel, we can reach them.
